items.prompt: In `a || b && c`, which part is grouped first?
items.explanation: `&&` binds tighter than `||`, so `b && c` resolves first and the `||` combines `a` with that result.

items.prompt: Which operator binds more tightly, `&&` or `||`?
choices: Neither; they are always read left to right
items.explanation: `&&` outranks `||`, the same way `*` outranks `+`.

items.prompt: Which arithmetic pair has the same strength relationship as `&&` and `||`?
items.explanation: Multiplication groups before addition, just as `&&` groups before `||`.

items.prompt: What do parentheses do in a boolean expression?
choices: Make the group inside resolve before the rest
Force the whole result to be true
Swap every `&&` for `||`
items.explanation: Parentheses override the default pecking order, exactly as in arithmetic.

items.prompt: With `a = true`, `b = false`, `c = false`, what is `a || b && c`?
choices: false
true
an error
items.explanation: `b && c` is false, then `a || false` is true because `a` is true.

items.prompt: With `a = true` and `b = true`, what is `!a && b`?
choices: true
undefined
false
items.explanation: `!a` is false, and `false && b` is false.

items.prompt: What does the `!` operator do to a value?
choices: Flips true to false and false to true
Keeps true and turns false into true
Combines two values into one
items.explanation: `!` is NOT: it reverses a single yes/no value.

items.prompt: A rule says 'not sick, and a pass or a wristband'. Which part needs the parentheses in code?
choices: The not-sick part
The pass-or-wristband part
The whole rule from end to end
items.explanation: Without parentheses around `hasPass || hasWristband`, the `&&` grabs `hasPass` alone and the wristband escapes the not-sick check.

items.prompt: Which fully parenthesized form matches how `!a || b && !c` is actually parsed?
items.explanation: `!` attaches to single values first, `&&` then groups `b` with `!c`, and the `||` joins `!a` to that group last.
items.reference:
Who grabs first
1️⃣ ! binds to what follows it
2️⃣ every && groups its two neighbours
3️⃣ every || comes last
🔒 parentheses override all of it
Why: && outranks || like * outranks +, so English grouping and code grouping can differ.
items.learnMore:
Precedence is a fixed pecking order

Strength of the operator decides grouping first. Reading order only breaks ties between operators of the same strength, which is why a rule spoken in English can group differently once typed.

Common mistake

Assuming a mixed &&/|| expression reads left to right like a sentence.
items.reflection: Think of a rule you have only ever heard spoken aloud (a house rule, a sign, a policy). Where could two reasonable people group its 'and's and 'or's differently?

items.explanation: The ticket is required in every case, so it must sit outside a group that holds the adult-or-accompanied alternatives. The other lines let a different part alone, or a ticket alone, satisfy the rule.

items.prompt: How many rows does a truth table need for 3 yes/no inputs?
items.explanation: Each input doubles the count: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

items.prompt: How many rows does a truth table need for 2 yes/no inputs?
items.explanation: 2 x 2 = 4: true/true, true/false, false/true, false/false.

items.prompt: What is a truth table?
choices: A list of every input combination with each rule's result
A list of the test cases a developer happened to try
A table of variable names and their types
items.explanation: Its defining property is that it covers all combinations, not a sample.

items.prompt: Why check every row instead of a few examples?
choices: A few examples can miss the one combination where the rules differ
Checking fewer rows always makes the program faster
The language requires a full table before it runs
items.explanation: Bugs hide in combinations nobody thought to try.

items.prompt: For two inputs, on how many of the 4 rows is `a && b` true?
items.explanation: `a && b` is true only when both are true, which is exactly 1 of the 4 rows.

items.prompt: For two inputs, on how many of the 4 rows is `a || b` false?
items.explanation: Only when both are false.

items.prompt: Two rules are equivalent when...
choices: they use the same variable names
they have the same number of operators
their result columns match on every row
items.explanation: Equivalence is about identical results for all inputs, not about how the rule is written.

items.prompt: How many rows does a truth table need for 4 yes/no inputs?
Two rules are compared on all 8 rows of a 3-input table and agree on 7. What can be concluded?
choices: Not equivalent; the one mismatched row is a concrete counterexample
They are equivalent for practical purposes, since 7 of 8 rows agree
They are equivalent unless the differing row is rare in real use
Nothing can be concluded until a ninth case is added to the table
items.explanation: Equivalence needs agreement on every row. One mismatch is a complete proof of difference and names the exact input to investigate.
items.reference:
Truth table
🔢 n inputs give 2n rows
📋 one column per rule being compared
🔍 equivalent = columns match on every row
🎯 one mismatch = a concrete counterexample
Why: a table covers every case, so no combination can hide the difference the way hand-picked examples can.
items.learnMore:
Why every row

Spot checks only prove the rules agree on the cases you thought of. The bug usually lives in a combination nobody thought to try, and the table is the only method that cannot skip one.

Common mistake

Declaring two rules equal because they agreed on the typical cases.
items.reflection: Pick a yes/no decision you make routinely (going outside, accepting an invitation). Which input combination would you most likely forget to consider?

items.prompt: Rule P is `a && b`; rule Q is `!(!a || !b)`. How do you most reliably decide whether they are equivalent?
choices: Test only `a = true, b = true`, since that is where P is true
Test two random rows and compare those
Check that both rules contain the same number of operators
Fill in all 4 rows for both and compare the result columns
items.explanation: Only a full table (or an equally exhaustive argument) rules out a hidden difference. Here the columns do match, so they are equivalent.

items.prompt: What is `!(A && B)` equal to?
items.explanation: Negating an AND flips it into an OR of the negated parts.

items.prompt: What is `!(A || B)` equal to?
items.explanation: Negating an OR flips it into an AND of the negated parts.

items.prompt: When a negation moves inside parentheses, what happens to `&&` and `||`?
choices: Each one flips to the other
Both stay the same
Both become `!`
items.explanation: The connective flips, and each piece is negated.

items.prompt: What is the exact opposite of 'it is raining and cold'?
choices: It is not raining or it is not cold
It is not raining and it is not cold
It is raining or it is cold
items.explanation: To break 'both', one failing is enough, so the opposite is an OR.

items.prompt: With `x = true` and `y = false`, what is `!(x || y)`?
choices: false
true
an error
items.explanation: `x || y` is true, and `!` flips it to false.

items.prompt: How would you say `!(isSick || isTired)` in plain words?
choices: Not sick and not tired
Not sick or not tired
Sick and tired
items.explanation: Negating an OR means neither holds: both must be false.

items.prompt: What is `!(A && B && C)` equal to?
items.explanation: The law extends to any number of terms: AND flips to OR and each term is negated.

items.prompt: True or false: `!(A && B)` is the same as `!A && !B`.
choices: True; negation applies to each piece only
False; the operator must flip to `||`
True, but only when `A` and `B` are both true
items.explanation: They differ whenever exactly one of A and B is true.

items.prompt: Which is equivalent to `!(a && (b || c))`?
items.explanation: The outer AND flips to OR, giving `!a || !(b || c)`, then the inner OR flips to AND, giving `!a || (!b && !c)`.
items.reference:
De Morgan
!(A && B) is !A || !B
!(A || B) is !A && !B
↔️ the operator flips as the ! moves inside
⬇️ work from the top operator inward
Why: negating 'both' means 'at least one is missing', and negating 'either' means 'neither', so the connective must change.
items.learnMore:
Negation flips the connective

'Not (raining and cold)' means dry or warm. The top operator of the negated expression picks the row, then you repeat for whatever remains inside.

Common mistake

Negating each piece but keeping the original operator, which is wrong whenever exactly one piece is true.
items.reflection: Take a requirement you know, such as 'must have both X and Y'. Say its exact opposite out loud. Did you flip the 'and' naturally?

items.prompt: A teammate writes the opposite of `isOwner || isEditor` as `!isOwner || !isEditor`. For which inputs does this go wrong?

Only when both are false
Only when both are true
Never; the two forms agree on every input
items.explanation: With one true, the real opposite is false, but the teammate's version is true because one of the negated pieces is true. On both-true and both-false rows they happen to match.

items.prompt: In `false && f()`, is `f()` called?
choices: No, the result is already false
Yes, both sides always run
Only if `f()` returns true
items.explanation: `&&` stops as soon as a false operand makes the result certain.

items.prompt: In `true || f()`, is `f()` called?
choices: Yes, because `||` needs both sides
No, the result is already true
Only the first time
items.explanation: `||` stops as soon as a true operand makes the result certain.

items.prompt: In `true && f()`, is `f()` called?
choices: No, a true left side ends the evaluation
Only if `f()` is slow
Yes, because the left side did not settle the answer
items.explanation: A true left side of `&&` leaves the right side as the deciding factor, so it must run.

items.prompt: What does short-circuit evaluation mean?
choices: Stopping as soon as the result is determined
Evaluating the right side before the left
Skipping `!` operators
items.explanation: The rest of the expression is skipped once it cannot change the answer.

items.prompt: For side-effect-free parts, does short-circuiting change the final true or false?
choices: No, only whether the right side runs
Yes, it flips `&&` results
Yes, but only for `||`
items.explanation: The truth value is the same; the work done is different.

items.prompt: Why write `list.length > 0 && list[0].ok` in that order?
choices: The length check guards the risky part
Because `&&` must start with a number
Because the right side always runs first
items.explanation: On an empty list the right side is skipped and no error occurs.

items.prompt: In `a || b` with `a = true`, is `b` examined?
choices: Yes, always
No
Only when `b` is true
items.explanation: `a` already makes the whole expression true.

items.prompt: In `x && y`, if `x` is false, what is the result?
choices: true
whatever `y` is
false
items.explanation: No value of `y` can rescue an AND with a false operand.

items.prompt: Given `f()` counts its calls and returns true, `const r = false && f(); const s = true || f(); const t = true && f();` runs. What are the call count and values?
choices: `f` called three times; r is false, s is true, t is true
`f` called twice; r is false, s is true, t is true
`f` called once; r is false, s is true, t is false
`f` called once; r is false, s is true, t is true
items.explanation: Only the last line needs `f()`: the first is settled by false, the second by true. `true && true` is true.
items.reference:
Stopping early
🛑 false && ... skips the right side
🛑 true || ... skips the right side
➡️ otherwise the right side decides
🛡️ guard first, risky part second
Why: the right side only runs if the left side has not already settled the answer.
items.learnMore:
Same answer, different work

For pure true/false questions the final result never changes. What changes is whether the right side runs, which matters when it is slow, has side effects, or fails on bad input.

Common mistake

Believing the order of operands never matters because a truth table shows no difference.
items.reflection: In everyday routines you check a cheap or safe thing before a costly or risky one (looking for your keys before ordering a car). Where else does order protect you?

items.prompt: With an empty array `items`, what does `items.length > 0 && items[0].ok` produce?
choices: A TypeError, because both sides always run
true, because an empty list has nothing wrong
false, and `items[0].ok` is never read
undefined, because `ok` is missing
items.explanation: `0 > 0` is false, so the AND stops there. Reading `items[0].ok` would fail, but it is skipped.

`b && a` is the safe one because risky checks should run first

items.prompt: A brute-force check of 3 flags tries how many combinations?
items.explanation: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 combinations.

items.prompt: If one input row gives different results for two rules, what is proven?
choices: The rules are not equivalent
The rules are equivalent
Nothing, one row is not enough
items.explanation: A single disagreement is a complete proof of difference.

items.prompt: If two rules agree on every row, what is proven?
choices: They are equivalent
They might still differ on some row
Only that they share variable names
items.explanation: Every possible input was covered, so no difference remains.

items.prompt: What is a row where two rules differ called?
choices: A counterexample
A tautology
A short circuit
items.explanation: It is a concrete input that shows the rules are not the same.

items.prompt: Why can code check every case for yes/no inputs?
choices: The number of combinations is finite
Because booleans never change
Because loops skip duplicates automatically
items.explanation: n inputs give exactly 2 to the power of n rows.

items.prompt: What does the loop enumerate?
choices: Every true/false combination of the inputs
Only the inputs seen in production
Only the inputs that make the rule true
items.explanation: Production data would be a sample, not a proof.

items.prompt: Two rules agree on 6 of 8 rows. Are they equivalent?
choices: No, two rows still disagree
Yes, most rows agree
Yes, if the disagreements are rare
items.explanation: Equivalence needs all rows to match.

items.prompt: In the loop, what does `buggy !== fixed` detect?
choices: A row where the two rules disagree
A row where both rules are true
A row that has already been checked
items.explanation: It is true exactly when the two results differ.

items.prompt: Two access rules differ on exactly 2 of 8 rows. The same extra condition `&& !isSuspended` is appended to both, adding a fourth input. How many of the 16 rows now disagree?
choices: 2 of 16, since a suspended user is refused by both
1 of 16, since suspension removes one of the original rows
4 of 16, since every original disagreement doubles
8 of 16, since half the rows now involve suspension
items.explanation: When `isSuspended` is true both rules are false, so they agree. When it is false, the original 2 disagreements remain.
items.reference:
Brute-force proof
🔁 loop over every true/false combination
⚖️ compare both rules on each row
❌ any mismatch = counterexample, proven different
✅ zero mismatches on all rows = proven equivalent
Why: the input space is finite and small, so you can cover all of it instead of sampling.
items.learnMore:
What a check proves

A proof covers exactly the rows it enumerated. Skipping part of the table can only ever show agreement on that part, never equivalence overall.

Common mistake

Restricting the loop to 'realistic' inputs and treating a clean result as a full proof.
items.reflection: Think of a claim you believed after seeing a few examples. What would 'checking every case' have looked like, and was it actually possible?

items.prompt: Rules X and Y agree on every row of a 3-input table. A fourth input `d` is added to X only, as `X && d`. Is the new X equivalent to Y?

No, they differ on any row where `d` is false and Y is true
Yes, because adding an input to one rule cannot change its result
No, but only on rows where `d` is true and Y is also true
items.explanation: With `d` false the new X is always false, so any row where Y is true is a disagreement. Agreement on the old table said nothing about the new input.

That the rules are equivalent, since `isOwner` is a minor input
That the buggy rule is the correct one, since it matched
Only that they agree when `isOwner` is false
items.explanation: A proof covers only the rows enumerated. The bug appears when the visitor is both sick and wearing a wristband, which this loop skipped.
items.reference:
Brute-force proof
🔁 loop over every true/false combination
⚖️ compare both rules on each row
❌ any mismatch = counterexample, proven different
✅ zero mismatches on all rows = proven equivalent
Why: the input space is finite and small, so you can cover all of it instead of sampling.
items.learnMore:
What a check proves

A proof covers exactly the rows it enumerated. Skipping part of the table can only ever show agreement on that part, never equivalence overall.

Common mistake

Restricting the loop to 'realistic' inputs and treating a clean result as a full proof.

items.explanation: The first condition applies to everyone, so it stays outside; the either/or pair goes in parentheses so the `&&` applies to the whole group.

items.prompt: The pool admits a visitor when `!isSick && (hasPass || hasWristband)`. Implement `isRefused(isSick, hasPass, hasWristband)` that is true exactly when entry is refused. Rewrite it with De Morgan's laws: do not put `!` in front of a parenthesized group.

tests.description: no `!` applied to a parenthesized group (use De Morgan)

items.explanation: Negating the top `&&` gives `isSick || !(hasPass || hasWristband)`, and negating the inner `||` gives `!hasPass && !hasWristband`. The tests cover all 8 rows, so only a correct derivation passes.
items.reference:
Rewrite by De Morgan
🔝 find the operator at the top of the negated group
↔️ flip it and negate each part
🔁 repeat on any group still under a !
🧪 confirm with every truth-table row
Why: each step applies one known law, so the result is provably the opposite instead of probably the opposite.
items.learnMore:
Derive, then verify

The derivation gives the form and the enumeration gives the proof. Code that only negates the pieces will pass some tests and fail the rows where exactly one piece is true.

Common mistake

Pushing the ! onto each variable but leaving the original && and || in place.

items.prompt: A club admits a guest when `(isAdult && hasId) || isVip`. Implement `shouldReject(isAdult, hasId, isVip)` that is true exactly when the guest is turned away, without putting `!` in front of a parenthesized group.

tests.description: no `!` applied to a parenthesized group (use De Morgan)

items.explanation: The top operator is `||`, so it flips to `&&`: `!(isAdult && hasId) && !isVip`. The inner `&&` then flips to `||`, giving `(!isAdult || !hasId) && !isVip`.

items.prompt: A document is published when `!isDraft && (isApproved || !isUrgent)`. Implement `needsReview(isDraft, isApproved, isUrgent)` that is true exactly when it is not published, without putting `!` in front of a parenthesized group.

tests.description: no `!` applied to a parenthesized group (use De Morgan)

items.explanation: Flip the outer `&&` to `||`, then the inner `||` to `&&`. Note `!isUrgent` negates back to `isUrgent`, so the result is `isDraft || (!isApproved && isUrgent)`.
